newsitem.title: USA: White House seeks to play down Jones court case.
newsitem.headline: White House seeks to play down Jones court case.

text.p: The White House did its best to play down the Supreme Court's hearing on Monday on whether the sexual harassment suit by Paula Jones should be allowed to proceed while President Bill Clinton is in office.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry referred reporters to Clinton's personal lawyer Robert Bennett, encouraged them to read the legal briefs filed in the case and for the most part replied in single sentences when pressed on the matter.
The court's nine justices considered for the first time the question of whether a sitting president may face civil legal action seeking damages for events that took place before he took office.

The court, which heard hour-long arguments by opposing lawyers, is focusing on when Jones's lawsuit may go forward, not the merits of her allegations that Clinton made unwanted sexual advances in 1991 in a Little Rock hotel room when he was governor of Arkansas and she was a state employee.
A ruling is due by the end of the court's term in June.
McCurry was generally terse as he discussed the matter. Asked if Clinton had any comment on the suit, the spokesman replied: "None that he shared with me."

Clinton, asked on Friday if the hearing would be a distraction, said, "I don't have any control over what anyone else does; I can only control what I do. It's not going to cause me any difficulty because I'm going to do my job here."

The White House wants to focus attention on the constitutional issue rather than on the suit's allegations. And with Clinton's inauguration on Jan. 20, it is keen to focus on his second-term agenda rather than on the Jones case.

Clinton spent his day on presidential business, awarding military Medals of Honour and working on his inaugural address. McCurry said the timing of the awards ceremony, which showed off Clinton in his role as commander in chief, had nothing to do with the Jones case.
Asked why Clinton had time to vacation but not to face a lawsuit, McCurry said any president was too consumed by the unpredictable burdens of office to defend himself in a civil case.

"The argument is much more that the constitutional duties of the president go with him 24 hours a day," he said. "Beyond that I'm not going to attempt to restate the arguments that Mr. Bennett and others argued effectively before the court."
McCurry's circumspection contrasted with public statements by Jones' lawyers, who went on television repeatedly to argue that Jones' case deserved to go forward.

One Jones lawyer, Joseph Cammarata, told reporters, "It's never too late to settle," suggesting if Clinton apologised, expressed regret for his conduct, and said that Jones did nothing wrong, "that gets close to where we need to be."
McCurry referred questions about a settlement to Bennett.

There have been efforts to settle the case out of court, once before it was filed and again in June before the Supreme Court decided to hear Clinton's appeal that the lawsuit should be delayed, lawyers have said.
